hints: Start at the outside edge of the leaf section and work inwards. The outermost single layer of cells has a different job from all the photosynthetic cells inside.
Look at cell shape in the middle layers. One layer has tall, tightly packed, column-like cells full of chloroplasts, while the other has rounded, loosely packed cells with large air spaces.
Match each label to its position - A points to the tall columnar layer just inside the upper surface, B points to the outer boundary layer, C points to the loose layer with air spaces below.
walkthrough:
Picture the standard leaf plan**
Think of a leaf in section from top to bottom. The very outside is a protective skin one cell thick. Just inside that on the upper side is a layer of long thin cells standing upright like fence posts, packed with chloroplasts for maximum light capture. That is palisade mesophyll, and label A points exactly there in both Fig. 1.1 and Fig. 1.2.

Separate skin from filling**
Label B points to the small, clear cells forming the continuous outer boundary. That single outer layer secretes the cuticle and protects the leaf, so it is epidermis. Label C points deeper inside to the irregular rounded cells with obvious white air spaces between them. That loose tissue allows diffusion of gases to and from stomata, so it is spongy mesophyll.
Final answer: A = palisade mesophyll; B = epidermis; C = spongy mesophyll.

hints: Compare the overall shapes first. One leaf section forms a deep U-shape with a sheltered hollow underneath, the other is almost circular in section. Only compare what you can actually see.
Look closely at the lower surface and the layers just inside the outer skin. Check for fine hair-like projections and for whether there is one outer layer or an extra supporting layer beneath it.
For each difference state both sides clearly, for example Erica has ... whereas Cedrus has ... Focus only on water-conserving features, not on palisade or spongy mesophyll in general.
walkthrough:
Spot the rolling and hairs in Erica**
In Fig. 1.1 the leaf curls under to enclose a large central chamber on the lower side. That is where most stomata are, sheltered from wind. Lining that chamber you can see fine hairs or trichomes. They trap moist air so the water potential gradient from leaf to air stays shallow and less vapour diffuses out. Fig. 1.2 shows no such rolling and no hairs.

Spot the strengthening and shape in Cedrus**
In Fig. 1.2 look just inside the small outer epidermal cells. There is a second layer of larger pale cells - the hypodermis - which helps support and reduce water loss. Erica does not show this. Also the whole Cedrus section is compact and almost circular, a needle-type shape. That gives a low surface area to volume ratio, so less surface for evaporation compared with the flatter rolled blade of Erica.

Write paired differences**
Keep to visible xerophytic features only and always give both sides. For example: Erica has a rolled leaf whereas Cedrus does not; Erica has trichomes whereas Cedrus does not; Cedrus has a hypodermis whereas Erica does not. Any three such paired points gain full credit.

Final answer: Erica v Cedrus, any three: Erica has curled / rolled leaf with enclosed lower surface, Cedrus does not; Erica has hairs / trichomes lining groove, Cedrus has none; Erica lacks hypodermis, Cedrus has hypodermis / extra cell layer below epidermis; Cedrus has cylindrical / needle-shaped leaf with low surface area to volume ratio; Erica has thicker cuticle / larger epidermal cells.

hints: Think about what the leaf must gain in the light for photosynthesis that it does not need in the dark, and which pore controls entry of that gas.
Remember the main route for water vapour loss. Compare diffusion through a wide open pore with diffusion through a waxy waterproof layer.
Link day and night to open and closed pores. Explain why open pores in the day inevitably mean more water loss even though the plant is trying to gain carbon dioxide.
walkthrough:
Why pores must open in the day**
Photosynthesis needs carbon dioxide and light. In the day guard cells open the stomata so carbon dioxide can diffuse in to the mesophyll for fixation. At night there is no light, so no photosynthesis and no need for carbon dioxide uptake, and stomata close.

Why open pores mean water loss**
An open stoma is a direct diffusion pathway from the moist air spaces inside the leaf to the drier air outside. Water vapour therefore escapes rapidly by diffusion down its water potential gradient. The cuticle is waxy and almost waterproof, so when stomata are closed at night only a tiny amount of water is lost through the cuticle. That is why transpiration is a consequence of gas exchange and is much greater during the day.

Final answer: Stomata open in the day and close at night; open to allow carbon dioxide in for photosynthesis in light, no need at night; most water vapour is lost through open stomata, very little is lost through the cuticle, so transpiration rate is higher in day.
